So, it's been a, you know, fast-moving environment even earlier this year when, you know, we had tensions rising in the Middle East, inflation expectations picked up not only domestically but abroad, and at one point, the market was actually pricing in a cash rate that may have been closer to 5% at one point.

headline: Pendal assesses US equity market concentration and valuation risks, noting that improved ROE and earnings revisions provide partial justification for elevated Shiller P/E.
reasoning: The ten largest AI-related companies now comprise 41% of the S&P 500, with bears pointing to historical precedent of equivalent concentration at previous market peaks and elevated long-term valuation metrics such as the Shiller P/E near its tech-wreck high. However, the counter-argument is that the S&P 500's 12-month forward EPS have been revised up 17% this calendar year even as the index rose ~9%, meaning the market P/E has actually fallen. Returns on equity for the S&P 500 have stepped up to 20-22% versus a prior 30-year range of 12-20%, driven by mega-cap stocks with global customer bases, providing greater justification for current valuations than existed in 1999.
quote: The ten largest AI-related companies now comprise 41% of the S&P 500 and bears point to the historic precedent of equivalent levels of concentration at previous market peaks. They also point to warning signs in longer-term valuation metrics. The Schiller P/E (the price over the average real earnings over 10 years) is near its previous high of the tech-wreck – as is the price/book ratio of the MSCI USA index. The counter to this is that these measures do not capture the shift in earnings and returns on equity, particularly from tech sector. For example the S&P 500 is up ~9% in US dollar terms this calendar year, but 12-month forward EPS have been revised up 17%, which means the market's P/E ratio has fallen despite the rise in the index. Returns-on-equity (ROE) for the S&P 500 have also stepped-up in the last three years to a range of 20-22% (and are currently at the high end), compared to a range of 12 to 20% over the previous 30 years.
